title: Joint Coverage Regions: Simultaneous Confidence and Prediction Sets
authors: Edgar Dobriban, Zhanran Lin
read_level: full text (parts: setup and multiplicity passage, intersection-based JCR results)
finding: Defines regions that jointly cover a fixed parameter and an unobserved new data point, unifying a Wald-type confidence interval with conformal prediction. It states that using the same data for both tasks makes joint error control harder and requires a multiplicity correction such as Bonferroni or a purpose-built joint region, and gives split-data versions. It is iid and single-sample: no clusters, no survey design, no PPI rectifier and no allocation of a labelling budget, but it is the only source found that addresses the validity of reusing one sample for an interval and a prediction set.

title: Model-assisted estimation as a unifying framework for estimating the area of land cover and land-cover change from remote sensing
authors: Stephen V. Stehman
read_level: abstract only (publisher page text via search tool; CrossRef metadata)
finding: Treats map-assisted area estimation as model-assisted estimation, which is a difference or regression estimator with the map as the predictor, and says one probability reference sample can serve area estimation and map accuracy assessment at once. The second use is estimating accuracy parameters of the predictor, not building prediction sets for unlabelled units, and no split or allocation of the reference sample between the two uses is studied.

title: Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change
authors: Pontus Olofsson, Giles M. Foody, Martin Herold, Stephen V. Stehman, Curtis E. Woodcock, Michael A. Wulder
read_level: abstract only (publisher page text and excerpts of a hosted copy via search tool; CrossRef metadata)
finding: Good-practice guidance in which one reference sample under a probability design feeds both area estimates with confidence intervals and the map accuracy assessment. It shares labelled data between a design-based estimator and an assessment of the predictor, but the assessment is of population accuracy measures, not unit-level prediction sets, and the sample is not split or allocated between purposes.

title: Sample size calculation for small-area estimation
authors: Nicholas T. Longford
read_level: abstract only (StatCan catalogue page text via search tool)
finding: Sets the allocation of one sample across areas from stated inferential priorities, for direct, composite and empirical Bayes estimators, with a national quantity as a further goal. It allocates one budget across several inferential goals, but all goals are estimation of area or national means; no prediction set for units is a goal.

title: On sample allocation for efficient domain estimation
authors: G. Hussain Choudhry, J.N.K. Rao, Michael A. Hidiroglou
read_level: abstract only (excerpts of the StatCan PDF via search tool)
finding: Uses nonlinear programming to minimise total sample size subject to coefficient-of-variation tolerances for strata and for domains cutting across strata, and compares with compromise and Longford allocations. Several precision goals share one sample, but every goal is a domain or stratum estimator; no unit-level prediction intervals.

title: More with Less: Bethel Allocation and Precision-Preserving Sample Size Reduction via Hierarchical Bayes Modelling
authors: Siu-Ming Tam
finding: Finds the minimum sample meeting national and domain precision targets for several variables at once (Bethel allocation), then reduces it further with hierarchical Bayes small area models. One budget serves many estimation goals, but no prediction sets for units and no reuse question.

title: Power Allocations: Determining Sample Sizes for Subnational Areas
authors: Michael D. Bankier
read_level: secondary (CrossRef metadata; described in the Statistics Canada 2009 rare-subpopulation article 12-001-X 2009002 11036 and the UN household survey handbook chapter VI)
finding: Per the secondary sources, a power allocation that compromises between proportional allocation (best for the national estimate) and equal allocation (best for subnational estimates). One budget, two estimation goals; no prediction sets.

title: Optima and Proxima in Linear Sample Designs
authors: Leslie Kish
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A (General)
read_level: secondary (CrossRef metadata; Kish compromise allocation described in the UN household survey handbook chapter VI)
finding: Cited by the UN handbook as the source of the Kish compromise allocation between national and provincial estimates. Same type of multi-goal estimation allocation as Bankier and Longford; no prediction sets.

title: Optimal network design for spatial prediction, covariance parameter estimation, and empirical prediction
authors: Dale L. Zimmerman
finding: Contrasts site designs optimal for kriging prediction with designs optimal for estimating covariance parameters, finds the two goals largely antithetical, and proposes a hybrid criterion for prediction with estimated parameters. One set of measured sites serves estimation and prediction, which is the closest design-level analogue found, but it is model-based geostatistics with no design-based estimator, no conformal sets and no clusters.

title: Rectification Difficulty and Optimal Sample Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys
authors: Zikun Ye, Hema Yoganarasimhan
finding: Allocates a fixed budget of human respondents across survey estimation tasks when LLM predictions exist for all, using PPI's residual variance per task to give a closed-form allocation. It is a PPI budget allocation across several estimands, but every use of the labels is a PPI estimator; no prediction sets and no within-cluster structure.

title: Conformal confidence intervals with an application to small area estimation
authors: Li-Chun Zhang, Tiziana Tuoto
finding: Builds conformal confidence intervals for area means using a split-sampling design: the sampled areas are split by SRSWOR into a training part that fits the regression and a scoring part that calibrates the interval, with half-sample training as default and interval width nearly flat for training shares of 15 to 50 percent. The split is between fitting and calibration of one interval type, not between a population estimator and prediction sets, and it is area-level, not units within clusters.

title: Design-based conformal prediction
authors: Jerzy Wieczorek
read_level: abstract only, plus appendix B passage (via search tool)
finding: Derives design-based finite-sample coverage for conformal prediction under common survey designs. Its appendix notes that a prediction interval for new units of an already-sampled cluster can use that cluster's data alone, which is the within-donor set of E8. It does not pair the sets with a design-based estimator or allocate the sample between them.

title: Optimal Conformal Prediction for Small Areas
authors: Elizabeth Bersson, Peter D. Hoff
venue: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology 12(5):1464-1488
finding: Gives area-level conformal prediction regions for an unsampled unit in a small area whose conformity score uses indirect information from other areas, keeping area-level coverage while narrowing sets. It is the survey analogue of borrowing across clusters (as in HCP and GHCP) against the direct within-area set, but no population estimator shares the data and no budget split is studied.

title: Design-based individual prediction
authors: Li-Chun Zhang, Danhyang Lee
finding: Defines design-based inference about unobserved individual prediction errors from the sampling design combined with a cross-validation sample-splitting design. The same sample trains and assesses the predictor at the unit level, but it gives risk estimates, not prediction sets, and pairs them with no population estimator.

title: Design-unbiased statistical learning in survey sampling
authors: Luis Sanguiao Sande, Li-Chun Zhang
finding: Subsampling Rao-Blackwell method: a training subsample of the survey sample fits an ML model and the rest gives an exactly design-unbiased model-assisted total. It splits labelled units between model fitting and the estimator, not between an estimator and prediction sets.

title: Model-assisted estimation with a training subsample: a two-phase sampling approach with design-based variance estimation
authors: Maria Eugenia Riano
finding: Treats the training subsample as a second sampling phase and derives the variance of a model-assisted estimator from one realised partition. It shows that budgeting the training phase recovers lost interval coverage. The split is between training and estimation, with no prediction-set use.

title: On design-unbiased algorithmic Machine Learning
authors: Li-Chun Zhang, Siu-Ming Tam, Luis Sanguiao-Sande, Wesley Yung, Anders Holmberg
finding: Studies conditions for unbiased prediction or classification over a finite population from sampled training data, and unbiased assessment of out-of-sample performance under the known design. Population-level and unit-level aims share the design, but no prediction sets and no allocation between aims.

title: Defining Ad-Hoc Sampling Designs for Small Area Estimation
authors: Piero Demetrio Falorsi, Stefano Falorsi, Vincenzo Nardelli, Paolo Righi
finding: Minimum-cost allocation that controls the accuracy of a model-based small area estimator, plus a selection step that secures planned sample sizes for each random-effect level. Estimation goals only.

title: Optimal Designs for Prediction in Two Treatment Groups Random Coefficient Regression Models
authors: Maryna Prus
finding: Gives A- and D-optimality criteria for estimating the fixed parameters and for predicting the random effects of individual units in random coefficient models. Both goals are on one design, which mirrors the population-level versus cluster-level split, but the prediction target is a random effect, not a set for new units, and the setting is model-based.

title: Optimizing the allocation of trials to sub-regions in multi-environment crop variety testing
authors: Maryna Prus, Hans-Peter Piepho
finding: Allocates trials across sub-regions to optimise best linear unbiased prediction of genotype effects in each sub-region, under a linear mixed model. Allocation for cluster-level prediction; no design-based estimator or prediction sets.

title: Valid predictions of random quantities in linear mixed models
authors: Nicholas Syring, Fernando Miguez, Jarad Niemi
finding: Constructs prediction intervals for random quantities, such as effects at a new farm, in two-stage mixed models that are valid at any sample size, using inferential models. Group-level predictive validity without a budget split or a design-based estimator.

title: Conformal causal inference for cluster randomized trials: model-robust inference without asymptotic approximations
authors: Bingkai Wang, Fan Li, Mengxin Yu
finding: Replaces average-effect inference in cluster randomized trials with conformal prediction intervals for cluster-level and individual-level treatment effects. Shows both levels of sets from one trial, but no estimator shares the labels and no allocation is studied.

title: Improving Treatment Effect Estimators Through Experiment Splitting
authors: Dominic Coey, Tom Cunningham
read_level: abstract only (excerpts of an author-hosted copy via search tool; CrossRef metadata)
finding: Splits each experiment into two parts, one used to estimate a shrinkage or prediction relation and the other to estimate the effect, and derives an optimal splitting fraction. An econometric example of choosing how much of one sample goes to each of two roles, but both roles serve point estimation; no intervals for units.

title: Experimental Evaluation of Individualized Treatment Rules
authors: Kosuke Imai, Michael Lingzhi Li
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
read_level: abstract only (excerpts of an author-hosted copy via search tool; CrossRef metadata)
finding: Learns and evaluates an individualized treatment rule on the same experimental data through cross-fitting, with design-based (Neyman) variance for the evaluation metric, alongside the average effect. Reuses one sample for learning and inference by cross-fitting, not for prediction sets.

title: Two-Phase Sampling Designs for Data Validation in Settings with Covariate Measurement Error and Continuous Outcome
authors: Gustavo Amorim, Ran Tao, Sarah Lotspeich, Pamela A. Shaw, Thomas Lumley, Bryan E. Shepherd
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 184:1368-1389
finding: Optimal two-phase designs for choosing the validation subsample; the best design depends on which estimator will use it, with a small efficiency loss when a design built for a design-based estimator feeds a model-based one. Relevant as evidence that one labelled subsample serving two analyses carries a design compromise, but both analyses are estimation.

title: Uncertainty quantification for probabilistic machine learning in earth observation using conformal prediction
authors: Geethen Singh, Glenn Moncrieff, Zander Venter, Kerry Cawse-Nicholson, Jasper Slingsby, Tamara B. Robinson
finding: Introduces conformal pixel-level sets for Earth observation products and contrasts them with design-based area estimates that give only population-level intervals; its case study splits reference labels 80/20 into calibration and test. It places both uses side by side but does not design one reference sample for both.

title: Choice of Sample Split in Out-of-Sample Forecast Evaluation
authors: Peter Reinhard Hansen, Allan Timmermann
read_level: abstract only (EconPapers page via search tool)
finding: Shows that the split of a series into estimation and evaluation periods drives size and power of out-of-sample forecast tests, and gives a test robust to mining over split points. A split between estimation and predictive evaluation, not between a population estimator and prediction intervals.

title: Model-Assisted Survey Estimation with Modern Prediction Techniques
authors: F. Jay Breidt, Jean D. Opsomer
read_level: secondary (excerpt of the journal PDF via search tool)
finding: Review of model-assisted estimation with ML predictors, noting that survey data are used both for finite-population estimation and for model fitting. Background for the difference-estimator view of PPI; no prediction sets.

title: Optimal two-stage sampling for mean estimation in multilevel populations when cluster size is informative
authors: Francesco Innocenti, Math J.J.M. Candel, Frans E.S. Tan, Gerard J.P. van Breukelen
finding: Optimal numbers of clusters and units per cluster for a population mean under a cost constraint. The single-goal two-stage allocation that a joint design would extend.

title: How Synthetic Labels Improve Conformal Prediction: A Perspective on Conditional Coverage
authors: Qianyi Chen, Bo Li
read_level: full text (arXiv HTML; abstract, method roadmap, Corollary B.6 and discussion read, rest keyword-scanned)
finding: A small trusted labelled sample is split into two disjoint parts. One part is paired with synthetic labels in a prediction-powered (rectified) estimate of pinball risk to learn a score-quantile function, and the other is kept untouched for final conformal calibration. Corollary B.6 gives an oracle square-root rule for dividing a fixed trusted budget between the two parts. This is the nearest found to splitting one label budget between a PPI-type estimator and conformal calibration, but the PPI step serves learning, not a population estimand, and the split is disjoint, with no reuse of labels across the two goals.

title: Extending Prediction-Powered Inference through Conformal Prediction
authors: Daniel Csillag, Pedro Dall'Antonia, Claudio Jose Struchiner, Guilherme Tegoni Goedert
venue: arXiv preprint (v1, 17 Oct 2025); ICML 2026 listing reported in the round 10 ledger was not verified here
read_level: full text (arXiv HTML; abstract, section 2.1 and experiment setup read)
finding: One labelled calibration set calibrates a conformal set predictor by split conformal. The resulting sets on unlabelled points then bound a population mean or Z-estimand, with the miscoverage rate entering the bound (Lemma 2.1), and e-values give confidence intervals. So the same labels yield both valid prediction sets and a population interval, but the sets serve only as an intermediate imputation device. The paper has no budget split, no clustered or hierarchical design, and does not report the sets as a deliverable.

title: Generalized Hierarchical Conformal Prediction
authors: Soham Mallick, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen, Edgar Dobriban, Yonghoon Lee
read_level: full text (arXiv HTML; method, experiments and appendix D.2 read, rest keyword-scanned)
finding: GHCP gives prediction sets for a test group with o initial observations by donating a reference-group size. It uses the first floor(o/2) test-group points for a local mean merged with a global fit, and the rest for calibration. Its baselines are HCP, the Dunn et al. pooling and subsampling methods, and split conformal within the test group (Std-CP, in the ACS PUMS experiment). A keyword scan found no full conformal set from the test group's own data and no mention of labelling budgets or PPI. Within one purpose, the initial sample is split between fitting and calibration.

title: Provably Label-Efficient Conformal Prediction
authors: Andrew Ilyas, Joonhyuk Ko, Jingwu Tang, Steven Wu, Jiahao Zhang
finding: Labels are queried one at a time, and an online stopping rule balances the cost of calibration labels against expected set size while keeping the conformal guarantee. Its expected cost matches the best fixed calibration size in hindsight. It prices calibration labels for a single goal (prediction sets) and does not share them with any estimator.

title: Allocating Human Oversight in AI-Enabled Analytics
authors: Zikun Ye, Jiameng Lyu, Rui Tao
read_level: full text (arXiv HTML; abstract read, keyword scan for conformal and prediction sets)
finding: Allocates one shared human-label budget across many PPI++ estimation tasks with an upper-confidence-bound policy. Each label both rectifies its task's estimate and informs the next allocation, and the paper notes this dual role affects small-budget performance. The goals are all population estimates; the text has no prediction sets or conformal methods.

title: Design-based conformal prediction
authors: Jerzy Wieczorek
read_level: full text (arXiv HTML; sections 3.4, 5.2 and appendix B read)
finding: Derives design-based finite-sample coverage for conformal prediction under SRS, unequal-probability and stratified designs. For two-stage cluster samples it points to Dunn et al., and for an already-sampled cluster it uses that cluster's own data alone. It lists other survey uses of conformal sets but does not combine them with design-based estimation of population quantities from the same sample.

title: Conformal confidence intervals with an application to small area estimation
authors: Li-Chun Zhang, Tiziana Tuoto
read_level: full text (arXiv HTML; abstract and introduction read, rest keyword-scanned)
finding: Builds conformal-style confidence intervals for the expectations of in-sample outcomes under a known split-sampling design, applied to small areas, to fill the gap between regression confidence and conformal prediction. One conformal construction thus serves estimation-type targets, but the paper does not deliver prediction sets and population intervals together or discuss splitting a label budget.

title: Distribution-Free Prediction Sets for Two-Layer Hierarchical Models
authors: Robin Dunn, Larry Wasserman, Aaditya Ramdas
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 118(544):2491-2502 (venue from Google Scholar listing)
read_level: abstract only (arXiv PDF excerpt via search); venue secondary (Google Scholar)
finding: Gives conformal sets for a new group (pooling CDFs, subsampling, double conformal) and for a new observation from an observed group under two-layer hierarchical sampling. These are prediction-set pieces only, with no estimation goal or budget question.

title: Distribution-free inference with hierarchical data
authors: Yonghoon Lee, Rina Foygel Barber, Rebecca Willett
venue: arXiv preprint (cited as Lee et al. 2026 in GHCP)
finding: Defines hierarchical exchangeability and HCP, extending conformal and jackknife+ to grouped data, including a second-moment coverage property for repeated measurements. Prediction sets only.

title: Few-Shot Conformal Prediction with Auxiliary Tasks
authors: Adam Fisch, Tal Schuster, Tommi Jaakkola, Regina Barzilay
finding: Meta-learns nonconformity scores and quantile predictors over exchangeable auxiliary tasks so that a new task with a few labelled points gets tight sets. This is a few-shot set for a new group, analogous to a target donor with o labels, but it has no inferential target and no budget split.

title: Reliable Confidence Intervals for Information Retrieval Evaluation Using Generative A.I
authors: Harrie Oosterhuis, Rolf Jagerman, Zhen Qin, Xuanhui Wang
finding: Offers two alternative methods, one PPI-based and one based on conformal risk control, that use a small set of reliable annotations to put confidence intervals on IR metrics; the conformal variant can vary its intervals per query. They are alternatives on the same kind of label set, not a joint design, and the abstract states no budget split.

title: Semi-Supervised Risk Control via Prediction-Powered Inference
authors: Bat-Sheva Einbinder, Liran Ringel, Yaniv Romano
venue: arXiv preprint; IEEE TPAMI 2025 per a citing paper (secondary)
read_level: secondary (search-result excerpt of the arXiv PDF and citing paper arXiv:2505.21147)
finding: Uses a PPI estimator of risk, built from labelled and unlabelled calibration sets, to tune a risk-controlling prediction-set parameter. PPI serves the set calibration and there is no separate population inferential target.

title: On Optimal Data Splitting for Split Conformal Prediction
authors: Sayan Das and co-authors (full list not read)
read_level: abstract only (arXiv abstract page via search)
finding: Characterizes the training-calibration ratio that minimizes split conformal interval length. It splits one labelled sample between fitting and calibration for a single goal, not between inference and prediction sets.

title: Transductive conformal inference with adaptive scores
authors: Ulysse Gazin and co-authors (full list not read)
read_level: secondary (search-result excerpts of arXiv and PMLR PDFs)
finding: Gives the joint distribution of conformal p-values for m test points sharing one calibration set and bounds the false coverage proportion uniformly. This bears on many spots of one target donor sharing calibration labels, not on the PPI interval.

title: Optimal Conformal Prediction for Small Areas
authors: Elizabeth Bersson, Peter D. Hoff
venue: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology 12(5):1464-1488 (from a citing reference list, secondary)
read_level: secondary (search-result excerpts of the arXiv HTML; venue from arXiv:2605.29249 reference list)
finding: Area-level conformal prediction regions that borrow indirect information through a Bayes working model while keeping within-area coverage. Prediction regions only; no joint use with design-based estimation.

title: Cluster-Robust Prediction-Powered Inference
authors: David Broska, Michael Howes
finding: Closed-form cluster-robust standard errors for PPI++ that drop the requirement that each cluster be fully labelled or fully unlabelled. This is a PPI piece relevant to partly labelled clusters, with no prediction sets.

title: Extending Prediction-Powered Inference through Conformal Prediction
authors: Daniel Csillag, Pedro Dall'Antonia, Claudio Jose Struchiner, Guilherme Tegoni Goedert
read_level: abstract plus keyword scan of arXiv HTML full text
finding: A labelled calibration set is used to fit a split conformal set-predictor, and that set-predictor imputes the unlabelled pool so that a valid CI or e-value for a population parameter follows. One labelled sample therefore yields both a calibrated set-predictor and a population interval. Here the sets are a means to the interval, not a product for named target units. There is no clustering, no target-group sets and no split or allocation of the labelling budget between the two outputs.

title: How Synthetic Labels Improve Conformal Prediction: A Perspective on Conditional Coverage
authors: Qianyi Chen, Bo Li
read_level: abstract plus keyword scan of arXiv HTML full text
finding: The small trusted labelled sample is divided into disjoint roles. One part pairs trusted with synthetic outcomes to bias-correct a prediction-powered quantile learner, and an independent trusted split does the final conformalization. The paper gives a benefit-cost rule and studies sensitivity to the trusted-label budget. Both uses serve a single prediction set, so there is no population estimand, and the split is within conformal calibration rather than between inference and sets.

title: Reliable Wireless Indoor Localization via Cross-Validated Prediction-Powered Calibration
authors: Seonghoon Yoo, Houssem Sifaou, Sangwoo Park, Joonhyuk Kang, Osvaldo Simeone
finding: Limited labelled calibration data are reused through K-fold cross-prediction to fine-tune a predictor, estimate the residual bias of synthetic labels in PPI fashion, and calibrate risk-controlling prediction sets, with coverage kept. This shows that one labelled set can do both PPI-type debiasing and set calibration through cross-fitting rather than a split. The debiased quantity is a set-calibration risk, not a reported population parameter, and nothing is clustered.

title: Semi-Supervised Risk Control via Prediction-Powered Inference
authors: Bat-Sheva Einbinder, Liran Ringel, Yaniv Romano
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 47(12):11080-11090
read_level: abstract (arXiv); bibliographic details from PubMed listing
finding: Labelled hold-out data act as the PPI rectifier for a risk estimate made on unlabelled data, and that estimate tunes the threshold of a risk-controlling prediction set. The same labels therefore enter both a PPI estimator and a set calibration. Again the PPI estimate is internal to the set, so no separate population inference is delivered and no budget is divided between goals.

title: Synthetic Counterfactual Labels for Efficient Conformal Counterfactual Inference
authors: Amirmohammad Farzaneh, Matteo Zecchin, Osvaldo Simeone
finding: Synthetic counterfactual labels are added to an RCPS conformal calibration, with a PPI-informed debiasing step, to narrow intervals for individual counterfactual outcomes. PPI serves only the prediction interval. There is no population estimand and no budget allocation.

title: PERRY: Policy Evaluation with Confidence Intervals using Auxiliary Data
authors: Aishwarya Mandyam, Jason Meng, Ge Gao, Jiankai Sun, Mac Schwager, Barbara E. Engelhardt, Emma Brunskill
finding: One paper gives two interval methods for off-policy evaluation with augmented data: a conformal interval for the state-conditional value and a doubly robust or PPI-style CI for the average value. It is the nearest in pairing a unit-level conformal interval with a population interval. The abstract does not say whether the same labelled data serve both, and it does not split a budget or treat clusters.

title: Cluster-Robust Prediction-Powered Inference
authors: David Broska, Michael Howes
read_level: abstract plus keyword scan of arXiv HTML full text
finding: Cluster-robust PPI++ gives closed-form standard errors for partially labelled clusters, and the authors show that precision depends on the labelling design, few labels in many clusters against many in a few. They suggest pairing the formulas with a cost model to allocate labels across and within clusters, but do not derive one. The full text has no mention of conformal or prediction intervals, so a single goal is served.

title: Rectification Difficulty and Optimal Sample Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys
authors: Zikun Ye, Hema Yoganarasimhan
finding: One fixed budget of human labels is allocated across many survey estimation tasks using a PPI-based rectification difficulty, with a closed-form Neyman-type rule. It allocates one budget across several inferential goals, but all of them are point estimates or intervals for parameters. No goal is a prediction set.

title: Allocating Human Oversight in AI-Enabled Analytics
authors: Zikun Ye, Jiameng Lyu, Rui Tao
finding: A shared human-validation budget is allocated across weighted tasks with an upper-confidence-bound policy. Each acquired label both feeds tuned PPI estimation and updates the allocation. This is one budget for several estimation goals, with labels serving estimation and design at once, but there is no prediction-set goal.

title: Valid Survey Simulations with Limited Human Data: The Roles of Prompting, Fine-Tuning, and Rectification
authors: Stefan Krsteski, Giuseppe Russo, Serina Chang, Robert West, Kristina Gligoric
finding: A fixed budget of human responses is split between fine-tuning the LLM synthesizer and PPI-style rectification. Under a fixed budget, giving most of it to rectification works best. This is a budget split between two uses of labels, but both serve one population estimate and neither is a prediction set.

title: Provably Label-Efficient Conformal Prediction
authors: Andrew Ilyas, Joonhyuk Ko, Jingwu Tang, Steven Wu, Jiahao Zhang
finding: An online stopping rule picks the number of calibration labels by trading labelling cost against expected prediction-set size while keeping the conformal guarantee. It treats the calibration budget as a cost for one goal. There is no population inference and no clustering.

title: Generalized Hierarchical Conformal Prediction
authors: Soham Mallick, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen, Edgar Dobriban, Yonghoon Lee
read_level: abstract plus keyword scan of arXiv HTML full text
finding: GHCP uses o initial test-group observations together with reference groups for target-group prediction sets. The full text compares against HCP and against split conformal within the test group, noting that the within-group split gives trivial sets for small o, and an appendix adds baselines. The text has no mention of PPI, design-based inference or a labelling budget. This bears on round 8's open item about GHCP's baselines.

title: The Exceedance Design Effect: Effective Sample Size for Thresholds under Clustering
authors: Adam Noonan
finding: Derives the effective sample size of a conformal calibration quantile under clustered scores via a level-dependent exceedance correlation, and concludes that sampling breadth (more sources) beats depth (more per source). It is relevant to how m labels per cluster serve set calibration. It does not involve PPI or a joint design.

title: How Many Human Survey Respondents is a Large Language Model Worth? An Uncertainty Quantification Perspective
authors: Chengpiao Huang, Yuhang Wu, Kaizheng Wang
venue: arXiv preprint (SSRN 6131846; short version at ICML 2025 per authors' repository)
finding: Converts LLM-simulated responses into confidence sets for population parameters, with the number of simulated responses as the design choice. It concerns population inference only, with no prediction sets and no split of the human-label budget.

title: Stratified Prediction-Powered Inference for Hybrid Language Model Evaluation
authors: Adam Fisch, Joshua Maynez, R. Alex Hofer, Bhuwan Dhingra, Amir Globerson, William W. Cohen
venue: arXiv preprint (NeurIPS 2024 per a citing paper's reference list, secondary)
finding: Stratified PPI with an optimal allocation of the labelling budget across strata for one population parameter. It is the stratified analogue of regime B allocation, with no prediction-set goal.

title: Active Statistical Inference
authors: Tijana Zrnic, Emmanuel J. Candes
venue: arXiv preprint (ICML 2024 per the Semantic Scholar listing, secondary)
finding: Chooses which points to label under a budget so that PPI-type confidence intervals are as narrow as possible. It is the base for budgeted PPI design and serves a single inferential goal.

title: Accurate prediction in reconstructed spatial transcriptomes does not ensure valid biological discovery
authors: Lorenzo Testa, Jing Lei, Kathryn Roeder
finding: Calibrates computationally reconstructed spatial expression against measured genes before differential-expression testing, in the same domain as E8. It is about valid inference only, with no prediction sets and no label-budget design.

title: Prediction-powered inference for time series across space
authors: Shahzar Rizvi, David Burt, Vishwak Srinivasan, Renato Berlinghieri, Stefano Del Col, Tamara Broderick
venue: arXiv preprint (TS-LIMITS Workshop, NeurIPS 2026, per arXiv comment)
finding: One of two works citing Csillag et al. It gives HAC-type PPI intervals per spatial location for short labelled time series. There are no prediction sets and no budget split.
